summary: This note covers the war and armed forces powers that Article One of the United States Constitution gives Congress. Only Congress may declare war, though it has sometimes authorized presidential military action without a declaration. The note also covers Congress's power to raise and regulate armed forces and state militias, and its exclusive power to make rules for land and naval forces, including two post-World War II statutes.
one_line: Summarizes Congress's constitutional war and armed forces powers under Article One, including declarations of war, army funding limits, militia authority, and military justice.
key_facts: Under the War Powers Clause, only Congress may declare war.
Five wars have been declared in United States history: the War of 1812, the Mexican-American War, the Spanish-American War, World War I and World War II.
Some historians argue that the legal doctrines and legislation passed during the operations against Pancho Villa constitute a sixth declaration of war.
Congress may grant letters of marque and reprisal.
No appropriation made for the support of the army may be used for more than two years.
The two-year army appropriation limit was inserted because the Framers feared a standing army beyond civilian control during peacetime.
Congress may regulate or call forth the state militias, but the states retain the authority to appoint officers and train personnel.
Congress has exclusive power to make rules and regulations governing the land and naval forces.
The U.S. Supreme Court has often reaffirmed Congress's exclusive hold on this power, for example in Burns v. Wilson, 346 U.S. 137 (1953).
Congress used its military power soon after World War II to enact the Uniform Code of Military Justice to improve the quality and fairness of courts martial and military justice.
Congress also enacted the Federal Tort Claims Act, which had allowed military service persons to sue for damages.
The Supreme Court repealed the Federal Tort Claims Act section allowing military service persons to sue in a divisive series of cases known collectively as the Feres Doctrine.
The executive branch and the Pentagon have asserted an ever-increasing measure of involvement in military rulemaking.
